text:
American cities have undergone a fundamental transformation from 1980 to 2024, characterized by accelerating gentrification, widening economic inequality, deteriorating housing affordability relative to income growth, and the displacement of lower-income residents [Source: ev-1]. Since 1980, nearly 80% of the country’s under-45 population growth has concentrated in metropolitan areas with over one million residents [Source: ev-1]. However, this phenomenon remains geographically uneven [Source: ev-2]. The most intensive transformation occurred in specific metropolitan areas where over half of eligible tracts changed status. Portland saw 58.1% of its eligible tracts gentrify, representing 36 out of 62 eligible tracts [Source: ev-2]. Washington D.C. experienced a rate of 51.9%, or 54 out of 104 eligible tracts [Source: ev-2]. Minneapolis recorded a rate of 50.6%, which was 39 out of 77 eligible tracts [Source: ev-2]. Seattle had a rate of 50%, corresponding to 7 out of 14 eligible tracts [Source: ev-2]. Other cities with high gentrification rates include Atlanta and Virginia Beach at 46.2%, Denver at 42.1%, and Austin at 39.7% [Source: ev-2]. In contrast, major metros like Detroit (2.8%), Las Vegas (2%), El Paso (0%), and Arlington, TX (0%) experienced little to no gentrification among eligible tracts [Source: ev-2]. New York City had the highest raw number of gentrified tracts (128), despite a lower percentage rate of 29.8% due to its large total tract count [Source: ev-2].

Inequality has risen in cities since the 1980s, reaching record levels by 2018–2021 according to Federal Reserve data tracking over 3,140 inequality series [Source: ev-1]. Specific city-level metrics include New York City with a Gini coefficient of 0.5469 [Source: ev-1], Atlanta and Miami with Gini coefficients of approximately 0.57 [Source: ev-1], and New Orleans with a Gini coefficient of 0.56 [Source: ev-1]. Income ratios further illustrate this divide. This divergence is most acute on the West Coast; California cities exhibit price-to-income ratios between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-1].

Gentrifying tracts saw population increases (+6.5%) and became whiter, with the non-Hispanic white share increasing by an average of 4.3 percentage points while poverty rates dropped slightly (0.7 percentage point decrease) [Source: ev-2] [Source: ev-1]. Conversely, lower-income areas that failed to gentrify experienced population losses (-2.4%), increased minority concentration (non-white share change noted as -5.0 in table context implying relative increase or specific metric shift), and sharp rises in poverty, which climbed nearly 7% (specifically a 6.7 percentage point increase) [Source: ev-2] [Source: ev-1]. Educational gentrification is also evident, with urban areas now having 35% of residents holding bachelor's degrees or higher, compared to 31% in suburbs and 19% in rural areas [Source: ev-1]. This shift concentrated high-income professionals in urban cores, contributing to income polarization where urban centers house both top earners and low-wage service workers, unlike the more moderate distributions found in suburbs [Source: ev-1] [Source: ev-2]. Only Houston showed improvement, with a mere 1.1% gain in income outcomes [Source: ev-1].
